title: Hypoglycemia
wiki_lead:
Hypoglycemia (American English), also spelled hypoglycaemia or hypoglycæmia (British English), sometimes called low blood sugar, is a fall in blood sugar to levels below normal, typically below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L). Whipple's triad is used to properly identify hypoglycemic episodes. It is defined as blood glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L), symptoms associated with hypoglycemia, and resolution of symptoms when blood sugar returns to normal. Hypoglycemia may result in headache, tiredness, clumsiness, trouble talking, confusion, fast heart rate, sweating, shakiness, nervousness, hunger, loss of consciousness, seizures, or death. Symptoms typically come on quickly. Symptoms can persist after  blood-glucose levels are restored to normal.
The most common cause of hypoglycemia is medications used to treat diabetes such as insulin, sulfonylureas, and biguanides. Risk is greater in people with diabetes who have eaten less than usual, recently exercised, or consumed alcohol. Other causes of hypoglycemia include severe illness, sepsis, kidney failure, liver disease, hormone deficiency, tumors such as insulinomas or non-B cell tumors, inborn errors of metabolism, and several medications. Low blood sugar may occur in otherwise healthy newborns who have not eaten for a few hours.
Hypoglycemia is treated by eating a sugary food or drink, for example glucose tablets or gel, apple juice, soft drinks, or lollipops. The person must be conscious and able to swallow. The goal is to consume 10–20 grams of a carbohydrate to raise blood glucose levels to a minimum of 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L). If a person is not able to take food by mouth, glucagon by injection or insufflation may help. The treatment of hypoglycemia unrelated to diabetes includes treating the underlying problem.
Among people with diabetes, prevention starts with learning the signs and symptoms of hypoglycemia. Diabetes medications, like insulin, sulfonylureas, and biguanides can also be adjusted or stopped to prevent hypoglycemia. Frequent and routine blood glucose testing is recommended. Some may find continuous glucose monitors with insulin pumps to be helpful in the management of diabetes and prevention of hypoglycemia.

Definition
Hypoglycemia, also called low blood sugar or low blood glucose, is a blood-sugar level below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L).
Blood-sugar levels fluctuate naturally throughout the day, with the body normally maintaining levels between 70 and 110 mg/dL (3.9–6.1 mmol/L). Although 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) is the lower limit of normal glucose, symptoms of hypoglycemia usually do not occur until blood sugar has fallen to 55 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L) or lower. The blood-glucose level at which symptoms of hypoglycemia develop in someone with several prior episodes of hypoglycemia may be even lower.

grok_lead: Hypoglycemia, also known as low blood sugar, is a medical condition characterized by an abnormally low level of glucose in the blood, typically defined as a plasma glucose concentration below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L). Normal fasting blood glucose levels are 70â99 mg/dL (3.9â5.5 mmol/L). Severe hypoglycemia is often defined as a blood glucose level below 54 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L); for example, a level of 27.3 mg/dL is severely lowânot high glucoseâand requires immediate medical attention due to the potential for confusion, seizures, loss of consciousness, or coma if untreated. Symptoms may not appear until levels drop further, such as below 55 mg/dL. This condition disrupts the body's primary energy source for cells, particularly in the brain, and is confirmed by Whipple's triad: the presence of symptoms, documentation of low blood glucose, and resolution of symptoms upon glucose correction. While it most commonly affects individuals with diabetes due to medications like insulin or sulfonylureas, it can also occur in non-diabetics from various causes, potentially leading to serious complications if untreated, including seizures, coma, or death. Symptoms of hypoglycemia are broadly categorized into neurogenic (adrenergic) responses, such as shakiness, restlessness, sweating, rapid heartbeat, anxiety, hunger, nausea, and pallor, which arise from the release of counter-regulatory hormones like epinephrine, and neuroglycopenic effects, including confusion, irritability, dizziness, blurred vision, slurred speech, fatigue, headache, and in severe cases, seizures, loss of consciousness, or unresponsiveness due to inadequate brain fuel. These manifestations can vary by individual and may occur suddenly, especially during sleep (e.g., nightmares or night sweats) or progress rapidly in those with repeated episodes, potentially leading to hypoglycemia unawareness where warning signs diminish. The primary causes of hypoglycemia in people with diabetes include excessive insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents, skipped or delayed meals, increased physical activity without adjustment, or illness, while in non-diabetics, it may result from excessive alcohol consumption, critical illnesses, prolonged fasting, rare tumors like insulinomas, or certain hormone deficiencies. Risk factors encompass having diabetes (particularly type 1, with incidence rates of 62â320 episodes per 100 patient-years, or type 2 at about 35 episodes per 100 patient-years), using specific medications, kidney disorders, or post-bariatric surgery states. Treatment involves prompt restoration of blood glucose levels. For conscious individuals with mild to moderate hypoglycemia (typically below 4 mmol/L), consume 15-20 g of quick-acting carbohydrate (e.g., 4-5 glucose tablets, 200 ml of a sugary drink like Lucozade, or 5-6 jelly babies), wait 10-15 minutes, then recheck blood glucose; repeat the quick-acting carbohydrate if still below 4 mmol/L. Once blood glucose exceeds 4 mmol/L and symptoms improve, consume a longer-acting carbohydrate snack (e.g., a sandwich, fruit with crackers, or the next meal if due) if the next meal is more than 1 hour away. For severe hypoglycemia (unconsciousness, confusion, or inability to swallow), administer glucagon injection if available and trained to do so, call emergency services immediately, and position the person on their side if unconscious. Prevention strategies include regular blood glucose monitoring, balanced carbohydrate intake, medication adjustments, and education on recognizing early signs, often managed through an interprofessional healthcare team to minimize recurrence and complications like brain damage or accidents.
